stem: A nursing student asks why an arterial blood gas is preferred over a venous blood gas when direct assessment of arterial oxygenation is required. Which explanation is best?

options.A: PaO2 is an arterial measurement used to assess oxygenation, and arterial-venous differences are especially large for oxygen partial pressure.
options.B: Arterial sampling is used mainly for research and does not provide clinically useful oxygenation information.
options.C: Venous PO2 is interchangeable with arterial PaO2 for direct assessment of oxygenation.
options.D: The main purpose of arterial sampling is to measure glucose rather than blood gases.

rationale: Current NCBI StatPearls states that PaO2 from arterial blood provides information about oxygenation and that measurement of PaO2 is a primary reason for obtaining an arterial specimen because arterial-venous differences are most pronounced for PO2. Venous blood gases can provide useful acid-base information in selected contexts but venous PO2 is not interchangeable with arterial PaO2 for direct oxygenation assessment. A is therefore correct.
educational_objective: Explain why arterial rather than venous sampling is required when direct PaO2-based assessment of oxygenation is needed.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_document_title: Arterial Blood Gas Analysis: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Clinical Utility — StatPearls
source_locator: Introduction — ABG measures PaO2 and PaCO2; specimen-comparison paragraph — PaO2 measurement as primary reason for arterial sampling and largest arterial-venous difference for PO2; Clinical Significance
source_claim_supported: Arterial PaO2 directly assesses oxygenation; venous PO2 differs substantially from arterial PO2 and is not equivalent for direct oxygenation assessment.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Printed p.13, Reduction of Risk Potential — interpret diagnostic tests and laboratory findings
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — arterial blood gas versus venous blood gas

source_original.stem: A nurse is explaining the difference between an arterial blood gas (ABG) and a venous blood gas (VBG) to a nursing student, who assumes the two tests are basically interchangeable for every clinical purpose. The nurse should explain that ABG sampling instead:

options.A: Arterial sampling better assesses oxygenation because PaO2 requires arterial blood
options.B: Arterial sampling is used mainly for research rather than bedside oxygenation
options.C: Venous sampling provides an equivalent PaO2 for routine oxygenation assessment
options.D: Arterial sampling primarily measures glucose and electrolytes rather than gases

source_original.rationale: Arterial blood gas sampling reflects oxygenated, post-pulmonary blood, providing an accurate assessment of oxygenation status (PaO2) in addition to acid-base status, whereas venous blood gas primarily reflects tissue metabolism and has more limited direct use for assessing oxygenation, though it can still provide useful acid-base and some metabolic information in certain clinical contexts.
source_original.source_detail: PaO2/oxygenation requires arterial sampling; updated 2026 StatPearls, accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Updated the exact source date to July 5, 2026, narrowed the construct to direct PaO2-based oxygenation so useful VBG applications do not become a competing issue, and reduced difficulty from hard to easy.

audit_findings.source_authority: NCBI StatPearls updated July 2026; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.claim_audit: NCBI directly states PaO2 assesses oxygenation and is the primary reason for arterial sampling because PO2 differs substantially between arterial and venous samples.

distractor_audit.B: ABGs are standard clinical tools for oxygenation/ventilation/acid-base assessment.
distractor_audit.C: Venous PO2 is not equivalent to arterial PaO2.
distractor_audit.D: ABG is a blood-gas/acid-base test, not primarily a glucose test.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: VBG may be adequate for selected acid-base questions, but the stem specifically asks direct arterial oxygenation assessment, eliminating that overlap.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address the purpose/comparability of arterial sampling; answer depends on diagnostic knowledge.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential is appropriate for diagnostic-test interpretation.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read the July 2026 NCBI Introduction, arterial-versus-venous specimen discussion and Clinical Significance; challenged whether VBG could be considered interchangeable for pH/PCO2, narrowed the stem to PaO2 oxygenation, and confirmed A remained uniquely correct.
